design_detail: Two double-blind, placebo-controlled, within-person laboratory studies reported in one open-access paper, both described as sequence- and gender-balanced, in healthy volunteers aged 18 to 50 who had taken MDMA before. Study 1 (16 people, 8 men and 8 women, outpatient, four sessions at least a week apart) crossed MDMA 1.5 mg/kg as the hydrochloride (1.26 mg/kg as the base) or its placebo with the alpha-1 adrenergic inverse agonist prazosin 1 mg or its placebo, prazosin an hour before, with water intake limited to about 473 mL an hour; prazosin was the positive control, given because it is expected to release antidiuretic hormone (ADH). Study 2 (12 people, 6 men and 6 women, inpatient, two sessions at least a week apart, with standardised meals and a breakfast of 500 mg sodium or less) gave MDMA 1.5 mg/kg or placebo and then, an hour later, a water challenge of 20 mL/kg drunk within 30 minutes, with no other fluid for at least 6 hours. Outcomes: serum sodium and plasma ADH (both studies), copeptin (Study 2 only, at baseline and 2 and 3 hours), and MDMA and metabolite concentrations (Study 1 only). The two studies were then pooled into one model of four drug-by-water conditions. Doses are study conditions only. Mixed-effects models in R with participant as a random effect; repeated measures were generally reduced to summary measures (maximum or minimum) before analysis.
can_establish: That in these volunteers a single 1.5 mg/kg dose of MDMA lowered serum sodium while leaving measured ADH and copeptin unchanged, although the control drug prazosin did raise ADH; and that when the same people drank 20 mL/kg of water an hour after the capsule, serum sodium fell further after MDMA than after placebo (minimum sodium, F(1,9) = 13.2, p = 0.005).
cannot_establish: Anything about difficulty passing urine: urine was collected but no urine result of any kind is reported, urine osmolality was not measured and urine volume is never given, so this paper cannot speak to urinary retention or to passing less urine. It also cannot establish the mechanism (no rise in ADH or copeptin was detected, and the authors could not replace it with another measured pathway), a dose-response (one dose), how large the fall would be at the amounts and fluid intakes people reach at a party, that the pooled 'potentiation' is a within-person effect (the four pooled conditions come from two different studies with different people and settings), or anything about women in particular, since the sex comparisons were exploratory and under-powered.

sample.recruitment: Newspaper and online advertisements and word of mouth; a physician judged people healthy on medical questionnaires, laboratory screening and a physical examination (p. 2).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Healthy people aged 18 to 50 who had taken MDMA before. Excluded: DSM-IV dependence on MDMA or any other psychoactive drug except nicotine or caffeine; wanting to stop or cut down MDMA use; earlier adverse reaction to the study drugs; current drug treatment; current legal supervision; any current physical or psychiatric illness that the study drugs might complicate or that might prevent completion; body mass index above 30 or below 18 kg/m2; current or recent medicines that might interact (p. 2).
sample.demographics: Study 1: 8 men and 8 women, mean age 26.6, SEM 1.8, range 18 to 42; men weighed 75.3 kg (SEM 4.1, range 57.3 to 94.1), women 63.1 kg (SEM 3.6, range 52.7 to 81.4). Study 2: 6 men and 6 women, mean age 28.6, SEM 1.9, range 21 to 40; weights are not reported, although the dose and the water challenge were both per kilogram. Ethnicity, how much MDMA people had used before and the interval since last use are not reported for either study (pp. 3, 5).
sample.attrition: Study 1: 8 of 448 ADH samples and 8 of 448 serum sodium samples were not collected or not analysable. Study 2: 14 of 120 ADH samples (8 of them from placebo sessions) were lost to failures of temperature control and 1 of 72 copeptin samples was missing; two people, one man and one woman, vomited within 15 minutes of finishing the water challenge in their MDMA sessions and their data were excluded. No one is reported as dropping out (pp. 4, 5).
sample.selection_effects: Healthy, screened volunteers who had taken MDMA before, were not dependent, had no earlier bad reaction and had a body mass index between 18 and 30, dosed by weight in a laboratory or hospital ward with measured fluid. People most at risk of severe low sodium in real life, in particular young women dancing for hours and drinking freely, are not this sample, and the paper's own account of the clinical cases says they are mostly women under 30. Whether anyone took part in both studies is not stated.

exposure.measurement: Study drugs given by the investigators in opaque gelatin capsules (lactose as placebo), MDMA weighed as the hydrochloride salt and supplied by David Nichols at Purdue University, prazosin bought commercially and overencapsulated; MDMA, MDA, HMMA and HMA concentrations were measured in plasma in Study 1 before and 1, 2, 4, 8, 24 and 48 hours after dosing. A negative urine drug screen, and for women a negative pregnancy test, was required immediately before dosing (pp. 2-3).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Study conditions only. A single oral dose of MDMA 1.5 mg/kg as the hydrochloride (1.26 mg/kg as the base) or placebo, given between 10:00 and 10:30. Study 1 added prazosin 1 mg or placebo by mouth an hour before MDMA; the first two people (one man, one woman) received 2 mg prazosin, but standing-up low blood pressure lasted about 9 to 11 hours after MDMA, so the dose was lowered to 1 mg for the remaining fourteen. Fluid: Study 1 limited to about 473 mL an hour; Study 2 a single water challenge of 20 mL/kg drunk within 30 minutes an hour after the capsule, with no other fluid for at least 6 hours (pp. 2-3).
exposure.polysubstance: Only the study drugs; dependence on other drugs was an exclusion and a urine drug screen had to be negative before dosing. Tobacco, caffeine and alcohol use outside the sessions is not reported.
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Not stated as a required period; a negative urine drug screen immediately before each session is the only check reported. Sessions were at least a week apart (pp. 2-3).

comparison.controls: Placebo in the same people in both studies. Study 1 also had prazosin alone and prazosin with MDMA, prazosin acting as a positive control expected to raise ADH; Study 2 compared MDMA with water loading against placebo with the same water loading (pp. 2-3).
comparison.matching: Within person, sequence- and gender-balanced; no randomisation method is described and no test of a period or sequence effect is reported.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: No pre-session measure of hydration in Study 1, which the authors name as a limitation; thirst was not measured in either study; urine osmolality was not measured; past MDMA exposure is not reported.
comparison.controls_other_drug_use: Not applicable: the same people served as their own controls.

outcomes.instruments: Serum sodium on a Siemens Dimension RxL Max integrated chemistry system; plasma ADH by radioimmunoassay at a commercial laboratory (limit of detection 1.0 pg/mL, interassay and intra-assay coefficients of variation 5.4% and 7.1%, stated reference range 1.0 to 13.3 pg/mL); copeptin in Study 2 only by enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (limit of detection 32 pg/mL, coefficients of variation under 4%); MDMA and metabolites by the authors' gas chromatography-mass spectrometry method. Blood at baseline and 1, 2, 3, 4, 6 and 24 hours after dosing; urine pooled before dosing and over 0 to 8 and 8 to 24 hours (pp. 3).
outcomes.validity_norms: The assays are standard and their performance is reported. ADH is hard to measure reliably, as the paper's own introduction explains (it binds to platelets and handling changes the result), and the authors later say variability in their ADH assay may have made a drug effect hard to detect. Hyponatremia is defined in the introduction as serum sodium below 135 mEq/L.
outcomes.operationalization: Effects were analysed as summary measures: the maximum ADH or copeptin concentration and the minimum serum sodium concentration per session, with condition (and in additional models gender) as fixed effects and participant as a random effect; the pooled analysis modelled change in serum sodium from baseline by condition and time (pp. 3-5).
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: None. Editors' count of 12 principal analyses (Study 1: ADH, serum sodium, the ADH-sodium relationship, the pharmacokinetics-sodium relationship; Study 2: ADH, copeptin, the ADH-copeptin correlation, serum sodium, copeptin as a predictor of sodium; pooled: condition, time and their interaction), besides six time-point contrasts in the pooled model, a gender term added to several models and the pharmacokinetic table. Pairwise comparisons after a main effect used Tukey's method; nothing else was adjusted, and the gender models are described as exploratory because the sample limited power.
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Both studies were double-blind and the outcomes are laboratory assays, so knowledge of condition is unlikely to affect them. No check of the blind is reported, and 1.5 mg/kg of MDMA produces obvious effects.

analysis.effect_sizes: Study 1 (water limited): condition affected maximum log-transformed ADH (F(3,45) = 5.68, p = 0.002) but gender did not (p = 0.11); both prazosin conditions raised ADH against placebo (prazosin alone z = 3.46, p = 0.002; prazosin with MDMA z = 3.22, p = 0.004) while MDMA did not (z = 1.21, p = 0.589). Serum sodium: condition F(3,357) = 8.44, p < 0.0001, gender F(1,14) = 5.913, p = 0.0291, no interaction; MDMA alone t(357) = -4.05, p < 0.0001, and MDMA with prazosin t(357) = -3.50, p = 0.0005, lowered sodium against placebo, while prazosin alone did not; women had a lower minimum than men (t(14) = -2.43, p = 0.029), already visible at baseline. No relationship was detected between ADH and the sodium fall, nor between peak MDMA or HMMA concentrations and the sodium fall. Pharmacokinetics (Table 1, mean and SD): MDMA maximum concentration 241 ± 36 ng/mL in men and 222 ± 58 in women after MDMA alone, half-life 7.7 ± 2.1 and 7.7 ± 1.5 hours; no significant effect of gender or of prazosin on MDMA kinetics. Study 2 (water loading): minimum serum sodium fell further after MDMA than after placebo, F(1,9) = 13.2, p = 0.005 (editors' calculation: t = 3.63, and if the 10 people who contributed both sessions are assumed, a within-person standardised difference of about 1.1); MDMA changed neither ADH (F(1,15) = 0.113, p = 0.74) nor copeptin (F(1,9) = 0.019, p = 0.89); ADH and copeptin were only weakly related (Kendall's tau 0.164, T = 500, p = 0.068); copeptin and condition each predicted sodium at 2 and 3 hours (condition F(1,32) = 12.2, p = 0.001; copeptin F(1,32) = 4.22, p = 0.048) without an interaction; women tended to lower minimum values (F(1,10) = 3.93, p = 0.0755) with no interaction with condition; one woman reached a serum sodium of 127 mmol/L at 3 hours after MDMA without symptoms. Pooled across the two studies: condition F(3,278) = 19.5, p < 0.0001, time F(5,278) = 16.9, p < 0.001, interaction F(15,278) = 8.62, p < 0.0001, with the fall after MDMA plus water loading larger than the sum of the two separate effects at 2 to 4 hours (z = 3.56 to 5.19, p < 0.0005). No mean sodium concentration, mean fall or confidence interval is printed anywhere in the text or in a table; the time courses appear only in Figures 3 and 6.
analysis.covariates: Gender was added to several models as a fixed effect and is described as exploratory. Nothing else was adjusted for; body weight is not in any model, although both the dose and the water challenge were per kilogram.
analysis.preregistration_detail: No registration number, protocol or analysis plan is mentioned anywhere in the paper. The studies were run under an Investigational New Drug exception from the US Food and Drug Administration and approved by the California Pacific Medical Center Institutional Review Board.
analysis.selective_reporting: Urine was collected before dosing and over 0 to 8 and 8 to 24 hours in both studies, but no urine result appears anywhere in the paper; the authors list not measuring urine osmolality as a limitation without saying what the collected urine was used for. Self-report and computerised task measures from the same sessions are said to be reported in separate papers. No mean sodium values or intervals are printed, only figures and test statistics.
analysis.power: No power calculation. The authors say the sample size limited power and call the gender analyses exploratory, and they suggest that variability in the ADH assay and the modest size of the studies may be why no ADH effect was detected. The main water-loading comparison rests on 10 people who contributed both sessions.

interpretation_gap.results_show: With fluid limited (Study 1), MDMA lowered serum sodium by about 1 to 1.5 mmol/L at its lowest point compared with placebo (editors' approximate reading of Figure 3(a)), and did so without any detected rise in ADH, while the control drug prazosin raised ADH without lowering sodium. With a 20 mL/kg water challenge (Study 2), sodium fell in both conditions but further and for longer after MDMA, to about 133.5 to 134 mmol/L at 3 hours against about 137.6 mmol/L on placebo (editors' approximate reading of Figure 3(b)), and one woman reached 127 mmol/L without symptoms. No measured hormone explained the difference.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The title says MDMA impairs the response to water intake, and the abstract concludes that MDMA potentiated the ability of water to lower serum sodium and that low sodium is a significant risk when hypotonic fluids are drunk during MDMA use (p. 1). The within-person part of this, that sodium fell further after MDMA than after placebo with the same water load, is what Study 2 shows in 10 to 12 people. The 'potentiation' statistic is weaker than it reads: the four conditions in the pooled model come from two separate studies with different participants, settings (outpatient against hospital ward) and fluid regimes, so the test of non-additivity is partly a comparison between studies rather than within people, and the paper does not say whether anyone took part in both. The negative findings are reported fairly: the authors state plainly that they could not relate the fall to ADH or copeptin and that they did not establish a mechanism.

timeline.event: Henry and colleagues gave 40 mg MDMA to eight men and reported a rise in vasopressin with a small fall in serum sodium; the direct hormone measurement this paper could not reproduce
Hartung and colleagues described low sodium after MDMA in a United Kingdom poison-centre series, usually with a large fluid intake
Rosenson and colleagues reported low sodium in a California poison-centre series, mostly in women
Simmler and colleagues reported that 125 mg MDMA raised plasma copeptin at 60 and 120 minutes in women but not in men; this paper detected no copeptin effect (cited here as reference 31, not read)
Hysek and colleagues, 32 volunteers given 125 mg MDMA: no significant overall change in copeptin
This paper: sodium fell after MDMA in both studies, further with a water load, with no detected change in ADH or copeptin

replication.where_it_stands: That MDMA lowers serum sodium, and lowers it more when water is drunk, is consistent across the controlled studies read in this library and fits the clinical case and poison-centre series. The mechanism is not settled: an early eight-man study found a vasopressin rise, one study found a copeptin rise in women only, and this study and Hysek and colleagues found no hormone change. No study read here measured urine output or urine concentration after MDMA, so the common experience of finding it hard to pass urine remains untested by controlled work.

funding.funder: National Institutes of Health grants DA017716 and DA016776 and NIH/National Center for Research Resources UCSF-CTSI UL1 RR024131 (Acknowledgments, p. 9). MDMA was supplied free of charge by David Nichols of Purdue University (p. 3).
funding.declared_conflicts: The authors state they have no competing interests (p. 9). The disclosure section notes that the first author's address at publication was Genentech.
funding.affiliations_note: Friends Research Institute (Addiction and Pharmacology Research Laboratory), the University of California, Berkeley, and the intramural programme of the National Institute on Drug Abuse. Recorded as a flag for closer reading, not as a reason to discount the results.

what_would_settle_it: A larger registered study at more than one dose that measures what this one did not: urine volume and urine osmolality through the session, thirst, and body weight change, alongside sodium and copeptin, with the water load and the dose crossed in the same people so that potentiation is tested within person rather than across two studies; and, for the question people actually ask, a study that records how much and how often participants pass urine after MDMA and after placebo.

domains.note: Both studies are described as sequence- and gender-balanced, but no randomisation or allocation method is described, and the prazosin dose was changed from 2 mg to 1 mg after the first two people, so those two were not treated like the other fourteen.

Sessions were at least a week apart and MDMA's half-life was about 7.7 hours, so drug carryover is unlikely; no period or sequence effect is tested or reported, and in Study 1 hydration before each session was uncontrolled, which the authors name as a limitation.

Double-blind with lactose placebo, but 1.5 mg/kg MDMA is unmistakable and no check of the blind is reported. In Study 2 the two people who vomited after the water challenge did so in their MDMA sessions, and the drinking of 20 mL/kg could not be blinded.

Small losses in Study 1 (8 of 448 for each of ADH and sodium), but in Study 2 14 of 120 ADH samples were lost to temperature-control failures and unevenly so (8 from placebo), and the two people who vomited had their MDMA-session data removed, an exclusion tied to the effect being studied and in the direction of losing the most affected sessions.

Serum sodium is measured objectively and blind to condition. ADH is the weak measure: the paper's own introduction explains that it is hard to assay, the authors later blame assay variability for their negative result, and a seventh of the Study 2 samples were lost to temperature failures, so 'no ADH effect' is a weak negative. Methods call the analytes plasma sodium and plasma ADH while the results and figures call them serum.

No registration, protocol or analysis plan is mentioned. Urine was collected at three points in both studies and no urine result is reported. The analyses as described (summary minimum and maximum values) do not match the printed degrees of freedom in two places, and the pooling of the two studies reads as a further analysis rather than a planned one. Mean values and intervals are nowhere printed, so only the test statistics can be checked.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: The central comparison is strong in design: the same people, placebo-controlled, with an objective laboratory outcome, and the result (more sodium fall after MDMA with the same water load) is consistent with the clinical literature and sizeable. What sets the overall judgment is the reporting rather than the conduct: nothing was registered, urine was collected and never reported, the described analyses do not match their own degrees of freedom, and no mean or interval is printed. The paper may be cited for the direction and the approximate size of the sodium fall under these conditions, for the fact that a 20 mL/kg water load after MDMA took one person in ten below 130 mmol/L without symptoms, and for the absence of any detected ADH or copeptin rise. It may not be cited for a mechanism, for a dose-response, for quantified risk at a party, for the pooled 'potentiation' as a within-person result, or for anything at all about passing urine.

key_findings.finding: With fluid limited to about 473 mL an hour, both MDMA conditions lowered serum sodium against placebo (MDMA alone t(357) = -4.05, p < 0.0001; MDMA with prazosin t(357) = -3.50, p = 0.0005; condition F(3,357) = 8.44, p < 0.0001), while prazosin alone did not. Note: no mean values are printed. Editors' approximate reading of Figure 3(a), p. 6, where the four curves can be told apart by shade and markers: at 3 hours, MDMA alone about 137.9 and prazosin with MDMA about 138.4 mmol/L, against placebo and prazosin near 139.5, a difference of roughly 1 to 1.6 mmol/L. [The card said the four curves cannot be told apart; on the 300-dpi rendering they can.]
key_findings.locator: The 473 mL an hour limit in Materials and Methods, 2.3 Study 1 Design (p. 3); Results, 3.4 Serum Sodium, 1st paragraph (p. 5)
key_findings.note: No mean values are printed. Editors' approximate reading of Figure 3(a), p. 6: the two MDMA conditions reached about 138 to 138.5 mmol/L at 3 hours while the two conditions without MDMA stayed near 139.5 to 140, a difference of roughly 1 to 1.5 mmol/L; the four curves cannot be told apart individually in the printed figure.

key_findings.finding: MDMA did not raise antidiuretic hormone, while the control drug prazosin did: condition affected maximum ADH (F(3,45) = 5.68, p = 0.002), with prazosin alone (z = 3.46, p = 0.002) and prazosin with MDMA (z = 3.22, p = 0.004) above placebo but MDMA not (z = 1.21, p = 0.589).
key_findings.locator: Results, 3.3 ADH (p. 4, right column, continuing on p. 5); Figure 2 (p. 5)

key_findings.finding: In the water-loading study, serum sodium fell further after MDMA than after placebo given the same 20 mL/kg water challenge: minimum sodium F(1,9) = 13.2, p = 0.005.
key_findings.note: Editors' calculation: t = 3.63; taking the degrees of freedom to mean that 10 of the 12 people contributed both sessions, this is a within-person standardised difference of about 1.1. Editors' approximate reading of Figure 3(b), p. 6: both conditions started near 139 to 140 mmol/L; after the water the placebo curve reached about 136 mmol/L at 2 hours and recovered, while the MDMA curve fell to about 133.5 to 134 mmol/L at 3 hours and was still about 138 at 6 hours.

key_findings.finding: One woman reached a serum sodium of 127 mmol/L at 3 hours after MDMA with the water challenge, without symptoms; this is the only individual value given in the text and the only case the authors call hyponatremia, although by the paper's own definition (below 135 mEq/L, Introduction, p. 1) Figure 5 (p. 7) shows other values below 135 at 2 and 3 hours after both MDMA and placebo with the water load (editors' reading). [It was not 'the only case of hyponatremia in either study'.]
key_findings.locator: Results, 3.8 Serum Sodium, 1st paragraph, end (p. 5); the definition in Introduction, 1st paragraph (p. 1)
key_findings.note: The paper defines hyponatremia as serum sodium below 135 mEq/L (Introduction, p. 1).

key_findings.finding: In the water-loading study no significant effect of MDMA was detected on ADH (maximum concentration F(1,15) = 0.113, p = 0.74) or on copeptin (F(1,9) = 0.019, p = 0.89), the longer-lasting marker released with ADH; copeptin and condition each predicted sodium at 2 and 3 hours (condition F(1,32) = 12.2, p = 0.001; copeptin F(1,32) = 4.22, p = 0.048) with no interaction. [The source says 'did not detect'; 'changed neither' overstated the negative.]
key_findings.locator: Results, 3.7 ADH and Copeptin; 3.8 Serum Sodium

key_findings.finding: Pooling the two studies, the fall in sodium after MDMA with water loading was larger than the sum of the falls after water loading alone and after MDMA with restricted water, at 2 to 4 hours (z = 3.56 to 5.19, p < 0.0005); condition F(3,278) = 19.5, time F(5,278) = 16.9, interaction F(15,278) = 8.62.
key_findings.note: The four pooled conditions come from two different studies with different participants, settings and fluid regimes; whether anyone took part in both is not stated, so this test is partly between studies rather than within people.

key_findings.finding: Neither ADH nor the measured drug concentrations accounted for the fall in sodium: no significant relationship was detected between ADH and the sodium decrease, and peak MDMA and HMMA concentrations (and their interaction) did not appear to predict it significantly once condition was in the model. [Hedge restored.]

Women had a lower minimum serum sodium than men in Study 1 (t(14) = -2.43, p = 0.029), which the authors say did not appear to be a drug effect and was visible at baseline, and tended lower in Study 2 (F(1,10) = 3.93, p = 0.0755); no significant interaction of sex with condition was found in either study. Note: the authors call the sex models exploratory because the sample limited power. [Hedge restored.]
key_findings.note: The authors call the sex models exploratory because the sample limited power.

key_findings.finding: Prazosin, the positive control, raised ADH without lowering serum sodium (pp. 4-5). Editors' inference, not the authors' words: in this study a rise in measured ADH did not by itself lower sodium, and the sodium fall after MDMA occurred without a detected ADH rise.

MDMA pharmacokinetics were unaffected by prazosin or by sex: maximum plasma concentration after MDMA alone 241 ± 36 ng/mL in men and 222 ± 58 ng/mL in women, half-life 7.7 ± 2.1 and 7.7 ± 1.5 hours, with no significant effect of gender or condition on maximum concentration, area under the curve or half-life.
key_findings.locator: Table 1 (p. 4); Results, 3.2 MDMA and Metabolites (p. 4, continuing on p. 5)

key_findings.finding: Limitations the authors state: both studies used a single dose level; hydration before the outpatient Study 1 sessions may have varied; thirst was not measured, so whether MDMA makes people want to drink was not tested; and urine osmolality was not measured.

Two of the 12 people in the water-loading study, one man and one woman, vomited within 15 minutes of finishing the water challenge in their MDMA sessions, and those data were excluded; the procedures are otherwise described as well tolerated.

reporting_issues.issue: Urine was collected in both studies, pooled before dosing and over 0 to 8 and 8 to 24 hours (Methods, 2.8), but no urine result of any kind appears in the paper, and the limitations say only that urine osmolality was not measured.
reporting_issues.consequence: What the collected urine was used for is unknown, and the paper cannot be cited for urine volume or concentration. For the question of whether MDMA makes it harder to pass urine, this is the measurement that is missing.

reporting_issues.issue: The printed degrees of freedom do not match the analyses as described. The Study 1 sodium model is said to predict the minimum serum sodium concentration, which gives one value per person per session, that is 64 values and about 45 residual degrees of freedom (as in the ADH model, F(3,45)); the printed F(3,357) and t(357) instead fit a model over all six post-dose measurements (16 people by 4 conditions by 6 times, less the 8 unusable samples, less 16 participants and 3 condition terms, is 357; editors' reconstruction).
reporting_issues.consequence: The model behind the main Study 1 result is not the one described, so its p values cannot be reproduced, and a model over repeated measurements without a time term is a weaker test than the summary-measure analysis the Methods promise.

reporting_issues.issue: The degrees of freedom also differ between analyses of the same 12 people in Study 2: sodium F(1,9) and copeptin F(1,9), gender F(1,10), but ADH F(1,15). With 12 people and 2 sessions a summary-measure model has at most about 11 residual degrees of freedom, and 9 if the two excluded sessions are counted out.
reporting_issues.consequence: The ADH analysis cannot have been run on the sample as described. Since the absence of an ADH effect is one of the paper's two headline findings, the strength of that negative result cannot be judged.

reporting_issues.issue: The number of ADH samples in Study 2 is given as 120, but the Methods say blood was taken at baseline and 1, 2, 3, 4, 6 and 24 hours, which for 12 people in 2 sessions would give 168 samples (editors' arithmetic); 120 corresponds instead to five time points. The 448 samples in Study 1 do match 16 people, 4 sessions and 7 times.
reporting_issues.consequence: The sampling schedule in Study 2 differed from the one described, in an unstated way, so the timing of the ADH measurements relative to the water load is uncertain.

reporting_issues.issue: The Methods describe plasma sodium and plasma ADH (section 2.8), while the Results, the figures and the abstract report serum sodium and, in one place, serum ADH.
reporting_issues.consequence: Which specimen was actually used is unclear. Serum and plasma sodium are close but not identical, and the difference matters when values are compared with a clinical threshold of 135 mmol/L.

reporting_issues.issue: The sodium assay's quality-control statement gives two coefficients of variation ('0.74% and 1.11%, respectively') with only one analyte and one concentration named, and that concentration, 119 mg/dL, is about 52 mmol/L, far below any possible serum sodium.
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor, but the stated precision of the main outcome measure cannot be checked as printed.

reporting_issues.issue: No mean serum sodium value, mean change or confidence interval is printed anywhere: all sodium results are given as test statistics, with the time courses only in Figures 3 and 6.
reporting_issues.consequence: The size of the effect, which is what a reader needs, has to be read off a figure. The readings on this card are approximate and should be treated as such.

reporting_issues.issue: The two people who vomited after the water challenge did so in their MDMA sessions, and those sessions were excluded from analysis.
reporting_issues.consequence: Vomiting is both a drug effect and a route by which fluid is lost, so the excluded sessions are not missing at random; the direction of the resulting bias in the sodium estimate is not obvious and is not discussed.
